sessions.topic: Build a multi-node cluster with kind; identify control-plane Pods; deploy, scale and expose an app
sessions.outcome: Match each event in the cluster to the component that caused it.
sessions.story: When you first hear about Kubernetes, it sounds abstract until you actually spin up a cluster on your own machine. In this lab, we start with a blank terminal, wire up a 3-node cluster inside Docker using kind, peek into kube-system to see the control-plane Pods running, and then deliberately break things, killing a Pod and stopping a worker node, to watch Kubernetes heal itself.

storyArc.hook: Teammate: "Your nginx app runs fine in Docker on your laptop, can we run 3 copies across worker nodes so one crash doesn't take it down?"
storyArc.break: A single container dies permanently if it crashes or its host stops, and users have no way to reach it.
storyArc.fix: Spin up a 3-node kind cluster, deploy nginx with 3 replicas, expose it via a Service, and test Pod/node failures.
storyArc.verify: Delete a Pod and stop a worker container, watch Kubernetes reschedule Pods and serve nginx on localhost:8080.

sessions.topic: Trace 'kubectl create deployment' end to end using events, etcdctl, crictl and kubelet logs
sessions.outcome: Match each event in the cluster to the component that caused it.
sessions.story: We type `kubectl create deployment` in one second, and a container appears. Have you ever wondered what actually happened in between? Here we follow a single Deployment like a detective, watching the HTTP POST hit kube-apiserver, reading the raw key inside etcd, checking the Pod sandbox with crictl, and even forcing a 409 Conflict to see optimistic concurrency in action.

storyArc.hook: Teammate: "We ran kubectl create deployment and containers appeared, which component actually did what, and how does Kubernetes stop two edits from colliding?"
storyArc.break: Treating Kubernetes like a black box makes debugging control-plane delays or 409 Conflict errors a guessing game.
storyArc.fix: Trace one Deployment end to end using -v=6 HTTP logs, cluster events, etcdctl, crictl, kubelet journalctl, and iptables.
storyArc.verify: Collect proof of every handoff (API Server → etcd → Controllers → Scheduler → Kubelet) and trigger a real 409 Conflict.

sessions.topic: Write a first controller with client-go: informer, work queue and reconcile of a deleted object
sessions.outcome: Run a client-go controller that heals a deleted object and catches up after a restart.
sessions.story: In Lab 2 we watched Kubernetes' built-in controllers do their job. Today we build our own in Go with client-go. We start with a simple rule, every labelled Namespace gets a ConfigMap, and then test our own code by deleting objects, stopping the controller mid-work, running two copies at once, and discovering what happens when a label is removed.

storyArc.beat: Chapter 3: Teaching Kubernetes a New Rule
storyArc.hook: Teammate: "Every time we create a team namespace, someone forgets to add the welcome ConfigMap, can Kubernetes create and heal it automatically?"
storyArc.break: Manual setup drifts the moment someone deletes a ConfigMap or creates a namespace while automation is offline.
storyArc.fix: Write a Go controller using client-go informers, a rate-limiting work queue, and an idempotent reconcile() loop, plus cleanup on label removal.
storyArc.verify: Delete the ConfigMap, restart after downtime, run two controllers at once, and unlabel a namespace to verify cleanup.

sessions.topic: Read the scheduler source, list default plugins and diagnose Pending Pods from FailedScheduling events
sessions.outcome: Trace a scheduling failure message to the plugin and source line that caused it.
sessions.story: Everyone hits a stuck `Pending` Pod eventually. Instead of guessing what went wrong, we sparse-clone the real Kubernetes v1.37.0 scheduler source code, find the exact Filter and Score plugins, and then intentionally break scheduling five different ways so we can trace every `FailedScheduling` message straight back to the Go code that wrote it.

storyArc.beat: Chapter 4: The 2 AM Pending Pod Mystery
storyArc.hook: Pager alert: "New Pods are stuck Pending in the cluster! Is it out of CPU, missing a disk label, tainted, port-conflicted, or cordoned?"
storyArc.break: A Pending Pod sits idle with no node assigned until you read its Events and understand which scheduler filter rejected it.
storyArc.fix: Inspect Kubernetes v1.37.0 kube-scheduler source code, reproduce all 5 failure modes, and resolve each constraint (label, toleration, uncordon).
storyArc.verify: Match every FailedScheduling event to its exact plugin in Go and confirm Pods recover to Running once fixed.
